planting.note: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil after all danger of frost has passed.

directions: Hollyhill Black Beauty pairs near-black bronze foliage with single, deep maroon-red blooms held on tall, well-branched stems above the dark leaves. Its open, single flower form makes the yellow-tipped stamens stand out against the dark petals, and the contrast with the foliage carries the display even between flushes of bloom. Pinch young plants once they have three or four sets of leaves to promote branching and more flowering stems, and stake taller plants in windy sites. Gardeners choose it for landscape and border color rather than exhibition, since the dark-leaved single form reads well from a distance in mixed beds.

planting.note: Plant tubers eye-up, 4-6 inches deep, in full sun after the soil has warmed following the last frost.

directions: Twyning's After Eight is a compact bishop-type dahlia with near-black, finely cut foliage that sets off pure white single flowers with a small yellow eye. Its low, bushy habit and small flower size make it well suited to container growing and the front of a border, where the foliage color reads as a design feature even before it flowers. Pinch the growing tip early to build a bushier plant, and deadhead regularly to keep new buds forming through summer. Gardeners often grow it specifically for the dark-leaf, white-flower combination, which is unusual among compact bedding dahlias.

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil once soil has warmed after the last frost.

directions: Jescot Julie is an orchid-type dahlia with narrow, spoon-shaped petals that curl into tubes at the tip, giving each bloom a spiky, star-like look in shades of orange-bronze over a bright golden-yellow reverse. The two-toned effect is strongest in cooler fall weather, and the airy flower form contrasts with the dense doubles common among dinnerplate dahlias. Provide sturdy staking as it grows to full height, and cut regularly for bouquets, since it is a strong repeat bloomer once established. Its distinctive spoon-petal shape appeals to gardeners and flower arrangers looking for texture rather than the classic ball or decorative dahlia form.

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep after the last frost once the soil has warmed.

directions: Arabian Night is a long-grown decorative dahlia whose densely packed, velvety petals open deep maroon and darken toward near-black as blooms mature, especially in cooler weather. The medium-sized flowers hold their color well as cut stems, and the sturdy plant habit generally needs only light staking. Pinch the central growing tip early in the season to encourage branching, and cut or deadhead spent blooms often to keep the plant flowering into fall. Its old-fashioned, near-black decorative form makes it a reliable choice for gardeners wanting deep, moody color without the size or staking demands of a dinnerplate variety.

planting.note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, and stagger plantings every two weeks for a longer bloom season.

directions: Priscilla is a ruffled gladiolus with creamy white petals edged in soft pink and a yellow throat, a fragrant heirloom-style bicolor that has remained popular for cutting since its introduction. Plant corms in well-drained soil and stake or plant in blocks to support the tall flower spikes, which open from the bottom up over several weeks. Cut spikes for indoor arrangements once the lowest two or three florets show color, leaving at least four leaves on the plant to recharge the corm. In colder zones, lift and store corms after foliage yellows in fall, since Priscilla is not reliably winter hardy outside zone 8 and warmer.

planting.note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in full sun once soil has warmed after the last frost.

directions: Nova Lux is a long-cultivated gladiolus prized for its clear, saturated golden-yellow florets held on tall, straight spikes, with little of the muddiness seen in some other yellow varieties. Plant corms in well-drained soil and provide support in exposed sites, since the tall flower spikes can lean once heavy with open blooms. Harvest for cut arrangements when the bottom florets begin to open, and leave the foliage intact afterward so the corm can rebuild for next season. Its dependable, true-yellow color has kept it in commercial and hobbyist cut-flower rotations for decades, valued for brightening mixed bouquets.
